title: Bring Your Own Model to the GitHub Copilot SDK with C#
summary: The GitHub Copilot SDK gives your application an agent runtime. BYOK lets you keep that runtime while sending model requests to your own Microsoft Foundry or Azure OpenAI deployment. Here is the complete C# setup. The post Bring Your Own Model to the GitHub Copilot SDK with C# appeared first on .NET Blog .
content:
Hi,

I know, I keep coming back to the same theme on this blog: **agent harnesses**. In [Build Your Own AI Agent Harness in C#](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/build-your-own-ai-agent-harness-in-csharp-the-maf-claw-live-series/) we built one from scratch. In [From dotnet run to Foundry Hosted Agent in 3 lines of C#](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/from-dotnet-run-to-foundry-hosted-agent-in-3-lines-of-csharp/) we took an agent and hosted it. Today we use a harness we do not have to build at all: the one GitHub already ships, through the **GitHub Copilot SDK**.

One of the most popular questions we received during the **Let’s Learn GitHub Copilot SDK** sessions was:

> “Can I use the Copilot SDK with my own model deployment?”

The short answer is **yes**.

The longer answer is, the GitHub Copilot SDK gives your application the Copilot agent runtime, while `ProviderConfig` lets you route model inference to a provider you control. That provider can be any of the [providers officially supported by the Copilot SDK](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/auth/byok): OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, Microsoft Foundry Local, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as vLLM or LiteLLM. Today’s sample uses **Microsoft Foundry**, authenticated with Microsoft Entra ID or, when needed, an API key.

The complete sample is now part of [Generative AI for Beginners .NET](https://github.com/microsoft/Generative-AI-for-beginners-dotnet/tree/main/samples/CoreSamples/GitHubCopilotSDK-01-BYOK). It is a small .NET 10 console application: read configuration, create a BYOK provider, start the Copilot runtime, create one session, and ask one question.

[Get the complete BYOK C# sample](https://github.com/microsoft/Generative-AI-for-beginners-dotnet/tree/main/samples/CoreSamples/GitHubCopilotSDK-01-BYOK)

## What BYOK means in this sample

BYOK means **Bring Your Own Key**, but in this context the important idea is broader than the key itself: you bring your own model provider.

The Copilot SDK still supplies the runtime that manages the client, session, system message, and agent configuration. `ProviderConfig` changes the destination and authentication for model inference.

**BYOK is not customer-managed encryption keys**

In this article, BYOK means using your own model endpoint and credentials for inference. It does not refer to customer-managed encryption keys or a storage-encryption configuration.

The sample intentionally keeps the session minimal. It disables tools, skills, configuration discovery, and host Git operations so that the first run demonstrates one thing clearly: a Copilot SDK session can send a model request to your own Foundry-compatible deployment.

![Diagram of a .NET app routing Copilot SDK requests to Microsoft Foundry](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/feed/github-copilot-sdk-byok-diagram.svg)

*The runtime and the model provider are separate parts of the application.*

## The project

The sample is a regular .NET 10 console application. These are the packages it uses:

```
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <UserSecretsId>genai-beginners-dotnet</UserSecretsId>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Azure.Identity" Version="1.21.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="GitHub.Copilot.SDK" Version="1.0.11" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration" Version="10.0.3" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.UserSecrets" Version="10.0.3" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

`GitHub.Copilot.SDK` provides the .NET client for the Copilot runtime. `Azure.Identity` provides `AzureCliCredential`, which lets the sample reuse the identity from `az login`. The configuration packages load development-only secrets without putting endpoints or credentials in source control.

## Step 1: read the model configuration

The sample uses the shared User Secrets values already used by the repository:

```
// User Secrets keeps the endpoint and credentials outside the repository.
var configuration = new ConfigurationBuilder()
    .AddUserSecrets<Program>(optional: true)
    .Build();

// This sample uses the repo's shared AzureOpenAI secrets.
var modelName = GetRequiredValue(configuration, "AzureOpenAI:Deployment");
var endpoint = GetRequiredValue(configuration, "AzureOpenAI:Endpoint");
var apiKey = configuration["AzureOpenAI:ApiKey"]?.Trim();
```

There are two required values:

* `AzureOpenAI:Deployment` is the name of your model deployment in Microsoft Foundry or Azure OpenAI. Choose a deployment that supports the Responses API, because this sample uses `WireApi = "responses"`.
* `AzureOpenAI:Endpoint` is the Foundry or Azure OpenAI resource endpoint.

`AzureOpenAI:ApiKey` is optional. If it is not present, the sample uses Microsoft Entra ID through `AzureCliCredential`. If it is present, the sample sends it in the `api-key` header.

## Step 2: configure the provider

This is the core of the sample:

```
// Microsoft Foundry exposes an API compatible with OpenAI Responses.
var provider = new ProviderConfig
{
    Type = "openai",
    BaseUrl = NormalizeEndpoint(endpoint),
    WireApi = "responses",
    ModelId = modelName,
    WireModel = modelName,
    MaxPromptTokens = 8000,
    MaxOutputTokens = 512
};
```

The configuration tells the Copilot runtime how to communicate with the provider:

* `Type = "openai"` selects the OpenAI-compatible provider shape.
* `BaseUrl` points to the OpenAI-compatible API surface.
* `WireApi = "responses"` selects the Responses API.
* `ModelId` identifies the model to the Copilot runtime.
* `WireModel` is the model name sent to the provider.
* The token limits keep this small example bounded.

For a reasoning model, `MaxOutputTokens` includes reasoning tokens as well as the visible answer. The 512-token limit can be reached before the model produces any answer. Increase or omit the `MaxOutputTokens` override when using a reasoning deployment, then tune the limit for your workload.

In this sample, `ModelId` and `WireModel` have the same value. They are separate properties because the runtime-facing model identifier and the provider-facing model name do not have to be identical in every integration.

The endpoint helper accepts either the resource URL or a URL that already includes `/openai/v1/`:

```
static string NormalizeEndpoint(string endpoint)
{
    var candidate = endpoint.Trim();
    if (!Uri.TryCreate(candidate, UriKind.Absolute, out var uri) ||
        uri.Scheme != Uri.UriSchemeHttps ||
        string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(uri.Host))
    {
        throw new ArgumentException("The configured AzureOpenAI:Endpoint must be an HTTPS URL.");
    }

    // Accept the resource URL or a URL that already ends in /openai/v1.
    // Trimming first means a trailing slash does not need a separate check.
    var trimmed = candidate.TrimEnd('/');
    if (trimmed.EndsWith("/openai/v1", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
    {
        return trimmed + "/";
    }

    return $"{uri.GetLeftPart(UriPartial.Authority).TrimEnd('/')}/openai/v1/";
}
```

The helper also requires HTTPS. It is better to reject a malformed endpoint before creating a session than to discover it after the first model request.

## Step 3: use Entra ID by default

The default authentication path uses the Azure CLI login:

```
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(apiKey))
{
    // AzureCliCredential reuses the session created with `az login`.
    var credential = new AzureCliCredential();
    var scope = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default";
#pragma warning disable GHCP001 // BYOK auth callbacks are experimental in the Copilot SDK.
    provider.BearerTokenProvider = async _ =>
    {
        var token = await credential.GetTokenAsync(
            new TokenRequestContext([scope]),
            cancellation.Token);
        return token.Token;
    };
#pragma warning restore GHCP001
}
```

Before signing in, make sure your identity has the **Cognitive Services OpenAI User** role on the resource. Then run:

```
az login
```

`BearerTokenProvider` is a callback. The SDK can call it when it needs a token instead of receiving one token value that the application has to manage itself.

## Step 4: use an API key when one is configured

Some deployments or environments still require an API key. The sample supports that path without changing the rest of the provider configuration:

```
else
{
    provider.Headers = new Dictionary<string, string>
    {
        ["api-key"] = apiKey
    };
}
```

Set the optional secret:

```
dotnet user-secrets set "AzureOpenAI:ApiKey" "<your-api-key>"
```

When the value exists, the sample uses the `api-key` header and does not require `az login`. The console output reports only the authentication mode; it never prints the endpoint or the credential.

**Keep credentials out of source control**

Use User Secrets for local development, environment-managed configuration for deployed applications, and never paste an API key into the source file or a README.

## Step 5: start the Copilot runtime

The provider controls model inference, but the Copilot runtime is still required:

```
await using var client = new CopilotClient(new CopilotClientOptions
{
    Connection = RuntimeConnection.ForStdio("copilot"),
    WorkingDirectory = AppContext.BaseDirectory
});
await client.StartAsync(cancellation.Token);
```

This is an important distinction. BYOK does not mean “the Copilot SDK without Copilot.” The local Copilot CLI runtime still provides the orchestration process. BYOK changes where the model request goes.

**Prerequisites**

Install the .NET 10 SDK and the GitHub Copilot CLI, and make sure `dotnet --version` reports a .NET 10 SDK and `copilot --version` works. For the default Microsoft Entra ID authentication path, also install the Azure CLI and make sure `az --version` works. The API-key path does not require the Azure CLI. The sample starts the local Copilot runtime through `RuntimeConnection.ForStdio("copilot")`.

## Step 6: create a deliberately small session

The session configuration connects the model name and provider, then disables capabilities that are outside the scope of this first example:

```
// Disable tools, skills, and Git operations to isolate the model request.
await using var session = await client.CreateSessionAsync(new SessionConfig
{
    ClientName = "github-copilot-sdk-byok",
    Model = modelName,
    Provider = provider,
    SystemMessage = new SystemMessageConfig
    {
        Mode = SystemMessageMode.Replace,
        Content = "Answer every user question in English. Be concise and factual."
    },
    AvailableTools = [],
    Tools = [],
    EnableConfigDiscovery = false,
    EnableSkills = false,
    EnableHostGitOperations = false
}, cancellation.Token);
```

The empty tool collections and disabled features are intentional. They make the sample easier to reason about and safer to run while learning the provider configuration.

The system message also makes the output predictable for a multilingual live-learning sample. `SystemMessageMode.Replace` replaces the default system message instead of appending another instruction to it.

## Step 7: send one question

Finally, the application sends one prompt and waits for the final response:

```
var response = await session.SendAndWaitAsync(
    new MessageOptions { Prompt = question },
    TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3),
    cancellation.Token);

var content = response?.Data.Content;
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(content))
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException("The model returned an empty response.");
}

Console.WriteLine();
Console.WriteLine("Answer:");
Console.WriteLine(content);
```

The default question is:

```
What is Microsoft Foundry, and how does it relate to the GitHub Copilot SDK?
```

You can provide another question as command-line arguments:

```
dotnet run -- "Explain BYOK in one sentence."
```

## Run the sample

From the sample directory, configure the required values:

```
dotnet user-secrets set "AzureOpenAI:Endpoint" "https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com"
dotnet user-secrets set "AzureOpenAI:Deployment" "<your-deployment-name>"
```

Then use the default Entra ID path:

```
az login
dotnet run
```

The output looks like this:

```
Model: <your-deployment-name>
Authentication: AzureCliCredential
Question: What is Microsoft Foundry, and how does it relate to the GitHub Copilot SDK?

Answer:
<model response>
```

The sample prints the selected model and authentication mode, but not the endpoint or credentials.

## So, what did we actually learn here?

Honestly, the part I like most is how little code this takes. ![🙂](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f642.png)

The Copilot SDK runtime and the model provider are two different things, and once that clicks, the rest is easy. You keep the runtime that GitHub gives you: the client, the session, the system message, and the agent plumbing. Then you just point inference somewhere else. That “somewhere else” is your Foundry deployment, your OpenAI key, your local Ollama, whatever you need.

Entra ID is the default path here, and I think it should be. No key to rotate, no key to leak, no key to accidentally commit. `az login` and you are done. The API key branch is there for the cases where you really need it, and it stays out of the way until you configure it.

And the session is deliberately boring. No tools, no skills, no MCP, no Git access. That is on purpose: the first run has exactly one job, which is proving that your model is answering. Once you see that answer in the console, you have a working baseline.

That is the fun part. From here you can start adding things one at a time: tools, MCP servers, skills, approvals, and streaming. When something breaks, you will know exactly which piece broke it.

Go try it with your own deployment. ![🚀](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f680.png)

[Explore the complete GitHub Copilot SDK sample](https://github.com/microsoft/Generative-AI-for-beginners-dotnet/tree/main/samples/CoreSamples/GitHubCopilotSDK-01-BYOK)

Happy coding!

Bruno

Years ago, in a galaxy far, far away, my colleagues in support, Keith Elmore and Robert Dorr, built a tool called **ostress.exe**. For decades it transformed the way we reproduced customer issues for SQL Server. The engineering team used it, and up until now I've used it for demonstrations, books, and examples. Its magic was simple: ostress could simulate many concurrent users running SQL queries or scripts.

I decided to rethink ostress for today's SQL world, and the result is sqlsimtools, now in public preview at https://aka.ms/sqlsimtools. It's a free, open-source suite of workload simulation tools for SQL Server 2019, 2022, and 2025, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric. I've been building it for some time and using it at events and in demonstrations. Now I want everyone to have it.

The public preview includes:

* **sqlsim**: a native, ODBC-based command-line tool for Windows (x64 and ARM64) and Ubuntu Linux.
* **sqlpysim:** a Python version of sqlsim built on Microsoft's mssql-python driver, for Windows and Ubuntu Linux.
* **sqlsim Studio**: a self-contained local browser app that configures, runs, monitors, replays, and compares workloads using sqlsim or sqlpysim. It's available today on Windows x64.

I'm also looking for Private Preview testers for macOS, and for sqlsim Studio on Linux and Windows ARM64. If you'd like to help, request Private Preview access.

I'll be writing more posts on different parts of the tools, but here are my top 10 cool things you can do with sqlsimtools:

* Run any SQL query, script, or mixed workload
* Create your own benchmarks, load tests, and stress tests
* Configure, run, monitor, and compare workloads visually with sqlsim Studio
* Replay captured SQL Server activity
* Monitor workload performance live or after execution
* Run before-and-after experiments with detailed performance comparisons
* Test SQL Server, Azure SQL, and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric with flexible authentication
* Use native or Python tools on Windows, Linux, and macOS (Private Preview)
* Automate testing with JSON results and live event streams
* Build and run workloads with AI agents such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Cursor

Get started today at <https://aka.ms/sqlsimtools> . The easiest way to start is the all-in-one sqlsimtools package, which includes sqlsim Studio and both command-line tools. You can also download just the tool for your platform, or clone the repo and build it yourself. On Windows, unblock the ZIP before you extract it, because the tools aren't code signed.

sqlsimtools is an open-source project, not an official Microsoft product, and isn't covered by Microsoft support. For questions and ideas, join the conversation in GitHub Discussions ([microsoft/sqlsimtools · Discussions · GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/sqlsimtools/discussions)), and report bugs in GitHub Issues ([Issues · microsoft/sqlsimtools](https://github.com/microsoft/sqlsimtools/issues)). During Public Preview I'm not taking Pull Requests yet but file issues and as the project progresses, we will incorporate the PR process.

Bob Ward

# How to Coordinate Role-Based CLI Seats & Session Handovers for AI Agents: A Governance MCP Server in Python

In 2026, multi-agent software engineering swarms (Claude Desktop, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, Roo-Code, AutoGen) frequently operate directly on local repositories and shell environments. Teams deploy autonomous agents to build features, fix bugs, run test suites, and execute deployments.

However, operating multiple agent sessions in the same terminal environment quickly exposes three critical concurrency and governance hazards:

1. **Race Conditions & Write Collisions:** When two agent sessions attempt to run git commands, build artifacts, or modify configuration files simultaneously, uncoordinated processes overwrite each other, producing corrupt states or broken builds.
2. **Session Handover Amnesia:** When an agent session terminates—whether reaching its context window limit, hitting a timeout, or concluding its turn—the successor agent starts blind. Without an auditable **session handover ledger**, the new agent doesn't know what commands ran, what uncommitted changes exist, or what steps remain pending.
3. **Out-of-Domain Execution:** An agent tasked with CLI scaffolding (`domain:cli`) accidentally runs destructive database or cloud infrastructure commands without boundary enforcement.

To eliminate these hazards, we built **CliSeat**: an open Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in Python that enforces **role-based single-writer seat locks**, logs cryptographically hashed **session handover briefs** to an immutable SQLite WAL ledger, automatically reaps abandoned seats via heartbeats, and redacts sensitive credentials from command I/O.

## 🏗️ The System Architecture

CliSeat acts as an authoritative governance sidecar between your AI assistants and the host shell:

```
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |       AI Agent / LLM (Claude, Cursor, Swarm)  |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                          (MCP JSON-RPC Tools)
                                   v
           +-----------------------------------------------+
           |            CliSeat Pro MCP Server             |
           +-----------------------------------------------+
              /                    |                    \
             v                     v                     v
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
   | Single-Writer Seat|  | Handover Ledger   |  | Command Governor  |
   | Lock (domain:cli) |  | (SQLite WAL SHA256|  | & Secret Masking  |
   +-------------------+  +-------------------+  +-------------------+
             \                     |                     /
              +--------------------+--------------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                      +-------------------------+
                      |   Governed Shell I/O    |
                      +-------------------------+
```

## 1. Single-Writer Seat Dispatch: Enforcing Mutual Exclusion

Only one agent session should hold mutation rights over a specific architectural domain at any given moment.

CliSeat manages domain seats (`domain:cli`, `domain:db`, `domain:infra`):

```
class SeatManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seats = {}

    def claim_seat(self, seat_id: str, holder_session_id: str, lease_ttl_sec: int = 180):
        seat = self.get_or_create(seat_id)
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        # Reject if held by an active session
        if seat.status == "occupied" and not seat.is_expired():
            if seat.holder != holder_session_id:
                return {
                    "status": "rejected",
                    "error": f"Seat '{seat_id}' is already held by '{seat.holder}'.",
                    "seat": seat.to_dict()
                }
            # Renew lease if already held
            seat.last_active = now
            return {"status": "renewed", "seat": seat.to_dict()}

        # Grant exclusive lock
        seat.holder = holder_session_id
        seat.status = "occupied"
        seat.claimed_at = now
        seat.last_active = now
        return {"status": "claimed", "seat": seat.to_dict()}
```

If another session attempts to mutate the repository while `domain:cli` is occupied, the claim is rejected immediately with the current holder's session ID and remaining lease time.

## 2. Preventing Context Amnesia: The Handover Ledger

When an agent finishes its task or reaches token budget exhaustion, it must produce a structured sign-off brief.

CliSeat persists every handover to an atomic SQLite WAL database sealed with a SHA-256 state hash:

```
import sqlite3
import hashlib
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class HandoverLedger:
    def __init__(self, db_path: str = "ledger.db"):
        self.db_path = db_path
        self._init_db()

    def record_handover(self, seat_id: str, event_type: str, session_id: str, brief: str):
        entry_id = f"hnd_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}"
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

        # Generate tamper-evident cryptographic hash
        hash_payload = f"{entry_id}:{seat_id}:{event_type}:{session_id}:{brief}:{now}"
        state_hash = hashlib.sha256(hash_payload.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

        with sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, isolation_level=None) as conn:
            conn.execute("""
                INSERT INTO handover_ledger (entry_id, seat_id, event_type, session_id, brief, state_hash, created_at)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?);
            """, (entry_id, seat_id, event_type, session_id, brief, state_hash, now))

        return {"entry_id": entry_id, "state_hash": state_hash[:16], "timestamp": now}
```

When the next agent takes the seat, it simply calls `get_handover_history(seat_id="domain:cli")` to see:

* What previous agents completed
* Unfinished branch names
* Known issues or test failures
* Pending pull request links

## 3. Boundary Enforcement & Secret Masking

To prevent accidents and credential leaks, CliSeat intercepts terminal commands:

1. **Domain Whitelists:** An agent on `domain:cli` is allowed `git`, `npm`, `pip`, `pytest`, and `cargo`, but blocked from executing database or infrastructure mutations.
2. **Credential Redactor:** Masks GitHub PATs, AWS secret keys, Bearer tokens, and passwords from command arguments and output logs.

```
SECRET_PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{15,}", re.IGNORECASE), "Bearer [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?:ghp|gho|ghu|github_pat)_[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}", re.IGNORECASE), "[REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]"),
]

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    for pattern, replacement in SECRET_PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(replacement, text)
    return text
```

## 4. Configuring with Claude Desktop or Cursor

Adding CliSeat to your local AI environment takes seconds. Add the following to `claude_desktop_config.json`:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cliseat": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["-m", "cliseat.server"]
    }
  }
}
```

Available MCP tools:

* `claim_seat(seat_id, holder_session_id)`
* `heartbeat(seat_id, holder_session_id)`
* `release_seat(seat_id, holder_session_id, handover_notes)`
* `get_seat_status(seat_id)`
* `execute_domain_command(seat_id, holder_session_id, command_line)`
* `get_handover_history(seat_id, limit)`
* `reap_expired_leases()`

The open-source **CliSeat Lite** is available immediately on GitHub under the MIT license:

I used to understand Large Language Models mostly from the outside.

I knew terms like:

* Transformer
* Attention
* Embeddings
* Tokens
* Fine-tuning
* GPT
* LLM

But knowing the terminology is very different from understanding what actually happens inside a model.

So instead of only reading about LLMs, I decided to **build a small language model from scratch using PyTorch**.

The goal wasn't to build the next ChatGPT.

The goal was much more important for me as a learner:



## What I Built

The model starts with Shakespeare text and learns to predict the next character.

The basic pipeline is:

```
Text
  ↓
Character Tokenization
  ↓
Token Embeddings
  ↓
Transformer Blocks
  ↓
RMSNorm
  ↓
Grouped Query Attention + RoPE
  ↓
SwiGLU Feed Forward Network
  ↓
Final Normalization
  ↓
Language Model Head
  ↓
Next-token prediction
```

The model configuration I worked with was:

```
Vocabulary size:       65
Embedding dimension:   256
Transformer blocks:     4
Query heads:            8
KV heads:               2
SwiGLU hidden size:     680
Context length:         256
```

The important thing is that these aren't just names in a diagram. I implemented the pieces and followed the tensors through the model.

# 1. First Problem: How Does Text Become Numbers?

Neural networks don't understand strings directly.

So the first step was tokenization.

For this project, I used a **character-level tokenizer**.

For example:

```
"Hello"
```

can become something like:

```
[20, 43, 50, 50, 53]
```

The tokenizer maintains two mappings:

```
char_to_idx = {
    character: integer
}

idx_to_char = {
    integer: character
}
```

Then:

```
def encode(s):
    return [char_to_idx[c] for c in s]

def decode(ids):
    return "".join([idx_to_char[i] for i in ids])
```

The important lesson for me was simple:

> **Before a model can learn language, language has to become numerical data.**

The training examples are created by shifting the sequence by one position.

For example:

```
Input:  To be o
Target: o be or
```

So the model is continuously learning:

```
Given previous characters → predict the next character
```

This turns one sequence of length `N` into `N` next-token prediction examples.

# 2. RMSNorm — A Simpler Way to Normalize Activations

One component I learned about was **RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Normalization)**.

Traditional LayerNorm performs operations involving the mean and standard deviation.

RMSNorm simplifies this.

Conceptually:

```
x
 ↓
calculate RMS
 ↓
normalize x
 ↓
learnable scale
```

The implementation is roughly:

```
rms = torch.sqrt(
    x.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + eps
)

output = (x / rms) * weight
```

The interesting part is that RMSNorm only needs a learnable scale vector.

My takeaway:

> **Normalization isn't just a mathematical trick. It helps keep the values flowing through a deep network under control.**

The material compares RMSNorm with LayerNorm and notes its use in modern architectures such as LLaMA, Mistral, and Gemma.

# 3. RoPE — How Does a Transformer Know Where a Token Is?

This was one of the concepts I found most interesting.

A transformer needs positional information.

One approach is to add positional embeddings.

RoPE — **Rotary Positional Embeddings** — takes a different approach.

Instead of simply adding a position vector, RoPE rotates the Query and Key vectors.

The important intuition is:

```
Position 3 → Position 5
distance = 2

Position 7 → Position 9
distance = 2
```

RoPE allows the attention mechanism to capture this kind of **relative positional relationship**.

At a high level:

```
Query + position
Key + position
       ↓
rotations
       ↓
attention
```

The rotation is applied to pairs of dimensions:

```
(d0, d1)
(d2, d3)
(d4, d5)
...
```

and each pair gets its own rotation frequency.

The biggest lesson I took from this:

> **Position isn't just “where is this token?” — attention can benefit from understanding how far apart tokens are.**

# 4. GQA — Reducing Attention Memory

Next came **Grouped Query Attention (GQA)**.

This was especially useful because it showed me that modern LLM architecture isn't only about making models bigger.

It's also about making them **more efficient**.

Instead of giving every Query head its own Key and Value heads, GQA allows multiple Query heads to share KV heads.

In my model:

```
Query heads = 8
KV heads    = 2
```

So four Query heads share each KV head.

Conceptually:

```
Q0 ─┐
Q1 ─┤
Q2 ─┤──→ K0, V0
Q3 ─┘

Q4 ─┐
Q5 ─┤
Q6 ─┤──→ K1, V1
Q7 ─┘
```

This significantly reduces the size of the KV cache.

The implementation first projects Q, K and V, reshapes them into heads, applies RoPE to Q and K, and then expands the KV heads to match the Query heads.

This taught me an important engineering lesson:

> **AI engineering isn't only about model accuracy. Memory usage and inference efficiency matter too.**

# 5. Causal Attention — Why Can't the Model See the Future?

During training, the model shouldn't be allowed to cheat.

Suppose we're predicting:

```
The cat sat
```

When predicting the next token after `"The"`, the model shouldn't be able to look at `"cat"`.

That's why causal masking is used.

Conceptually:

```
       T0 T1 T2 T3

T0     ✓  ✗  ✗  ✗
T1     ✓  ✓  ✗  ✗
T2     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✗
T3     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓
```

Each token can attend to itself and previous tokens, but not future tokens.

The attention computation looks roughly like:

```
scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * scale

scores = scores.masked_fill(
    mask,
    float("-inf")
)

weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)

out = weights @ v
```

This made the phrase **“next-token prediction”** much more concrete for me.

# 6. SwiGLU — The Feed-Forward Part Isn't Just ReLU

Another component I implemented was **SwiGLU**.

A traditional feed-forward network can look like:

```
Input
  ↓
Linear
  ↓
ReLU
  ↓
Linear
  ↓
Output
```

SwiGLU introduces a gating mechanism.

It has two paths:

```
             ┌──→ SiLU ──┐
Input ───────┤            × ──→ Linear ──→ Output
             └──→ Up ────┘
```

The core operation is:

```
gate = F.silu(self.w_gate(x))
up = self.w_up(x)

output = self.w_down(gate * up)
```

The gate learns which information should be emphasized or suppressed.

The training material describes this as a gated dual-path feed-forward network, with SiLU on the gate path and element-wise multiplication controlling information flow.

# 7. Putting Everything Together

A transformer block in my implementation follows this pattern:

```
Input
  │
  ├── RMSNorm
  │
  ├── GQA + RoPE
  │
  └── Residual Add
          ↓
        x'
          │
          ├── RMSNorm
          │
          ├── SwiGLU
          │
          └── Residual Add
                 ↓
               Output
```

In code:

```
x = x + self.attention(
    self.attn_norm(x),
    rope_cos,
    rope_sin
)

x = x + self.ffn(
    self.ffn_norm(x)
)
```

This is a **pre-norm + residual** architecture.

The residual connection means the block learns a change to the existing representation instead of having to completely rebuild it at every layer.

# 8. The Complete Mini LLM

The complete model then becomes:

```
Character IDs
     ↓
Token Embedding
     ↓
Transformer Block × 4
     │
     ├── RMSNorm
     ├── GQA
     │    └── RoPE
     ├── Residual
     ├── RMSNorm
     ├── SwiGLU
     └── Residual
     ↓
Final RMSNorm
     ↓
Language Model Head
     ↓
Logits
     ↓
Softmax
     ↓
Next Character
```

The model uses weight tying between the token embedding and language-model head.

The complete architecture in the project uses 4 transformer blocks, 8 Query heads, 2 KV heads, and a 256-dimensional representation.

# 9. Training the Model

Once the architecture was ready, the next question was:

**How does it actually learn?**

The training loop follows the familiar deep-learning pattern:

```
Get batch
   ↓
Forward pass
   ↓
Calculate loss
   ↓
Zero gradients
   ↓
Backward pass
   ↓
Gradient clipping
   ↓
Optimizer step
```

The project used:

```
Batch size:      64
Learning rate:   3e-4
Optimizer:       AdamW
Training steps:  3000
```

The training code follows:

```
xb, yb = get_batch(...)

logits, loss = model(xb, yb)

optimizer.zero_grad()

loss.backward()

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(
    model.parameters(),
    max_norm=1.0
)

optimizer.step()
```

Gradient clipping is used to reduce the risk of exploding gradients during training.

# 10. Training Loss vs Validation Loss

One thing I don't want to overlook when building ML models is evaluation.

A model getting better on training data doesn't automatically mean it's generalizing well.

So we can compare:

```
Training loss
      vs
Validation loss
```

A growing gap between them can be a signal of overfitting.

During evaluation, dropout is disabled and gradients aren't needed:

```
@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss():
    model.eval()
    ...
    model.train()
```

The training material uses the train/validation loss gap as an indicator for overfitting.

# 11. Finally: Generating Text

After training, the model can generate new text.

The process is autoregressive:

```
Prompt
  ↓
Model
  ↓
Predict next token
  ↓
Append token
  ↓
Model again
  ↓
Predict next token
  ↓
Repeat...
```

For example:

```
"ROMEO:"
```

gets encoded into token IDs.

The model predicts the next character, adds it to the sequence, and repeats the process.

The generation code takes the logits from the **last position**, converts them into probabilities using softmax, samples the next token, and appends it to the sequence.

# 12. Temperature Controls Randomness

Another concept that became much clearer after implementing generation was **temperature**.

Lower temperature:

```
More predictable
Less random
```

Higher temperature:

```
More diverse
More random
```

For example:

```
T = 0.3 → conservative
T = 0.8 → balanced
T = 1.5 → creative
```

So temperature doesn't make the model “smarter”.

It changes how we sample from its probability distribution.

# What I Actually Learned From This Project

The biggest lesson wasn't memorizing what RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA and SwiGLU stand for.

It was understanding how the pieces connect.

Before this project, I could say:

> “Transformers use attention.”

Now I can explain:

```
Text
 ↓
Tokens
 ↓
Embeddings
 ↓
Q / K / V
 ↓
RoPE
 ↓
Causal Attention
 ↓
GQA
 ↓
Residual Connection
 ↓
SwiGLU
 ↓
Repeated Transformer Blocks
 ↓
Logits
 ↓
Probability Distribution
 ↓
Next Token
```

That difference is important.

**Knowing the vocabulary is not the same as understanding the system.**

# Why I Built This Instead of Only Using an LLM API

As someone preparing for an AI/ML engineering role, I think there is value in going one layer deeper.

Using:

```
response = client.chat(...)
```

is useful.

But understanding what happens underneath gives me a stronger foundation for:

* debugging ML systems
* reading research papers
* understanding model architectures
* optimizing inference
* experimenting with transformers
* explaining technical decisions during interviews

I don't expect a small Shakespeare model to qualify me for an LLM engineering role by itself.

But building it gave me something more valuable:

> **A mental model of how modern language models work.**

# My Biggest Takeaways

### 1. Build, don't just watch

Reading about transformers is useful.

Implementing one forces you to understand the tensor shapes and data flow.

### 2. Understand the “why”

Don't memorize:

```
RoPE
GQA
RMSNorm
SwiGLU
```

Ask:

```
Why is it there?
What problem does it solve?
What happens if I remove it?
```

### 3. Follow the tensors

One of the best ways I found to understand deep learning code is to constantly ask:

```
What is the shape here?
```

For example:

```
[b, seq, 256]
      ↓
[b, 8, seq, 32]
      ↓
attention
      ↓
[b, seq, 256]
```

### 4. AI engineering is more than model training

A good ML engineer needs to think about:

```
Data
↓
Architecture
↓
Training
↓
Evaluation
↓
Inference
↓
Efficiency
```

### 5. Projects become much more valuable when you can explain them

This is probably the biggest career lesson I took from this.

Don't just put:

> “Built an LLM using PyTorch”

on a resume.

Be able to explain:

> “I implemented character tokenization, causal next-token prediction, RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA with shared KV heads, SwiGLU, residual transformer blocks, AdamW training, validation loss evaluation, and autoregressive generation.”

That demonstrates actual understanding.

# What's Next?

This project gave me a foundation.

My next step is to move from:

**“I understand how the architecture works.”**

to:

**“I can build useful AI systems with it.”**

That means exploring things like:

* fine-tuning
* embeddings
* RAG
* vector databases
* evaluation
* inference optimization
* model deployment
* AI agents
* production ML pipelines

The goal isn't to learn every AI buzzword.

The goal is to **build things, understand them, and document what I learn.**

## Final Thought

I'm learning that the fastest way to improve as an AI/ML engineer isn't to wait until I know everything.

It's to:

**Learn → Build → Break → Debug → Explain → Share → Repeat.**

This small LLM project was one step in that process.

And I'm going to keep documenting the journey.

**Tech Stack:** Python · PyTorch · Deep Learning · Transformers · LLMs

**What would you recommend I build next — a RAG system, fine-tuned model, or an AI agent?**
